_comment: Ground-truth ZipVoice token ids, captured from sherpa-onnx - the independent implementation - with
model debug on. English reaches this model through espeak-ng grapheme-to-phoneme, and the shipped
lexicon.txt is Chinese-only, so there is no table these ids can be read out of. They were observed,
not derived, which is what makes them a valid target for our own phonemizer to reproduce.
Regenerate with:
dotnet run --project tools/zipvoice-oracle -c Release -- "Paint the sockets in the wall dull green." out.wav 2> debug.log
grep 'new sentence' debug.log
The prompt text spans two sentences (the comma splits it); its token list is their concatenation,
which is what sherpa feeds the encoder.
WARNING - THE REFERENCE CLIP AND ITS TRANSCRIPT DO NOT MATCH.
promptWav (the packaged prompt.wav) does NOT say what promptText claims. Whisper transcribes it as
"Today, I'm so happy. So, today is the first day.", and the English-only model refuses it outright as
"(speaking in foreign language)". ZipVoice is therefore told the clip contains words it does not, and
SPEAKS them at the start of every render - which is the preamble on all of this audio.
The pairing is left as it is ON PURPOSE, so earlier measurements stay reproducible, and because the
COMPARISONS built on it are still valid: both frontends are handed the same prompt. Its absolute word
error is inflated by roughly six points. For clean absolute numbers, build fixtures against a clip you
have an accurate transcript for:
dotnet run --project tools/zipvoice-fixture -c Release -- --file sentences.txt --out <dir> \
--prompt-wav <your.wav> --prompt-text "<exactly what it says>"
text: Paint the sockets in the wall dull green.
promptText: Some call me nature, others call me mother nature.
